thread.title_full: Neolithic cow's tooth found in 1924 may hold the key to understanding the origin of Stonehenge - NewsBreak

author: Somdatta Maity
title: Neolithic cow's tooth found in 1924 may hold the key to understanding the origin of Stonehenge - NewsBreak
text:
By Somdatta Maity ,
4 hours ago Neolithic cow’s tooth found in 1924 may hold the key to understanding the origin of Stonehenge Remains of a cow shed light on how Stonehenge may have been erected . Researchers analyzed a Neolithic cow's molar, and the chemical signatures indicate that it could have been involved in the transportation of the legendary stones. Insights regarding this investigation are published in the Journal of Archaeological Science . Researchers focused on the cow's third molar during their analysis, as this tooth specifically recorded events from the animal's second year of life. Through the investigation, researchers measured oxygen, carbon, strontium, and lead isotope levels present in the tooth, which hinted at the creature's environment, movement, and diet during the second year, especially in the six months between winter and summer.
Brown Cattle on Open Field (Representative Image Source: Pexels | Photo by Pixabay)
Discovery of Cow Remains The Neolithic cow's jawbone was unearthed in 1924 alongside bluestones in England, according to Popular Mechanics . Researchers discovered it buried in the south entrance, which was considered to be a revered ritual location by the ancient population. It implies that the cow was valued by the community, as it was buried in such a pivotal place. Further examinations revealed that the fossils dated between 2995 and 2990 B.C., aligning with the beginning of Stonehenge. To understand why the cow was so valued by the community, researchers conducted an isotope analysis. During the process, the team found out about the cow's role in the building of Stonehenge.
Photo of Stonehenge, London (Representative Image Source: Pexels | Photo by Samuel Wölfl) Origin of the Cow
Isotope analysis showcased that the cow was likely a female, nursing during the time of tooth formation, according to the BBC . The third molar, measuring around an inch, was divided into nine horizontal sections during the investigation. The results indicated that the animal came from Wales. Considering that it was buried beside Stonehenge, the finding also connects the monument to Wales.
Professor Jane Evans, from the British Geological Survey, claims that the team's assertion of a Wales connection is built on the fact that the isotope analysis points towards the cow grazing on the Palaeozoic rocks, which are found in Wales. Furthermore, the areas where these rocks are found are also the places where bluestones have been detected. Bluestones are constituents of Stonehenge , which further solidifies the connection. "We're beginning to see so many connections between Wales and Stonehenge. Not only is it the closest rock, but there are other links as well," she added.
Stonehenge monument. (Representative Image Source: Getty Images | Tetra Images)
Cow's Journey to Stonehenge Bluestones, apart from Wales, are also present in the Lake District and Scotland, which made it difficult for experts to trace Stonehenge back to a particular location. However, the new evidence from Palaeozoic rocks clearly paints Wales as the best candidate for the monument's origin. Researchers also supported the claim made in 2018 that cattle carried loads to help humans during the Neolithic times . Researchers believe this cattle, along with others, carried boulders from Wales to erect Stonehenge, near Salisbury in Wiltshire.
The quantity of carbon, oxygen, strontium, and lead isotopes revealed the animal's diet during those six months. Researchers found evidence that hinted that the cow ate food sources from different geological areas, and that its diet changed with seasons. It suggested that either the cow moved from one place to another, in between seasons, or that its winter fodder was imported to their home. Analysis of lead isotopes indicates that the cow was exposed to an older lead source between late winter and spring, compared to other times. This older lead was linked to Wales, while the others could have come from various places along the route.
Brown and White Cow (Representative Image Source: Pexels | Photo by Tobi) "The composition suggests the cow originated from an area with Palaeozoic rocks, such as the bluestones found in Wales, before moving to Stonehenge," the scientists added. "This is yet more fascinating evidence for Stonehenge's link with south-west Wales, where its bluestones come from," said Michael Parker Pearson, professor of British later prehistory at University College London (UCL). The evidence tracing the cow's beginning from Wales to end in Stonehenge indicates that it could have been involved in moving the boulders.
